usage: the default verb is 하다; spoken 요가하다 is fine, but never 운동하다
수업 = a class/lesson; 요가 클래스 (loanword) is interchangeable at studios
매트 is the fixed loanword for the mat; 깔개 (a Korean word for 'mat') is wrong here
-원(院) marks a small academy/clinic; same suffix as 학원, 병원
examples: 저는 요가를 좋아해요.
I like yoga.
the simplest frame: noun + 를 + 좋아하다, treating 요가 as a plain object
저는 일주일에 두 번 요가를 해요.
I do yoga twice a week.
일주일에 N 번 = N times per week; 에 marks the time-span the count happens within
회사 근처에 요가원이 새로 생겼길래 등록했어요.
A yoga studio newly opened near my office, so I signed up.
생기다 = (a place) comes into being/opens; -길래 = 'since (I noticed)', a casual reason
nuance: 요가 is the universal loanword from English 'yoga' (via Sanskrit); no Korean ever translates it. The reflex error is treating it like exercise and saying 요가 운동을 하다 — that doubles 'exercise/do', so just use 요가를 하다 or, colloquially, 요가하다. Compare it with 스트레칭 (stretching): 요가 is a whole disciplined practice with poses (동작/자세) and breathing, while 스트레칭 is just loosening muscles, so they are not swappable. A studio is a 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오 — never 요가집, because the homey suffix -집 is for eateries and shops, not for a class venue. One session is a 요가 수업 / 요가 클래스, and the gear is a 요가 매트.

mistakes: 요가 운동을 해요. → 요가를 해요.
Adding 운동(을) 하다 ('to do exercise') after 요가 is redundant because 요가 already names the activity; the bare 요가를 하다 / 요가하다 is what Koreans say.
Drop 운동: 요가를 해요 / 요가해요.
요가집에 다녀요. → 요가원에 다녀요.
The suffix -집 means a shop or eatery (e.g. 빵집, 고깃집), so 요가집 sounds wrong for a class venue; studios use the academy suffix -원.
Use 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오.

usage: the verb is 하다; 필테 is the chat abbreviation friends actually type
기구(器具) = apparatus; contrasts with 매트 필라테스 done on a mat
등록하다(登錄) = to register; classes are sold as prepaid packages
read 일대일; a private lesson, much pricier than group (그룹) classes
examples: 저는 필라테스를 해요.
I do Pilates.
the basic frame, naming the activity with the all-purpose verb 하다
요즘 자세 교정하려고 필라테스 다녀요.
I'm doing Pilates these days to fix my posture.
다니다 = to attend regularly; -(으)려고 = 'in order to', stating your goal
10회권 끊었는데 벌써 다 썼어요.
I bought a 10-session pass but I've already used it all.
N회권(回券) = an N-session ticket; 끊다 = to buy (a ticketed pass), not 사다
nuance: 필라테스 transliterates the founder's name 'Pilates' and is abbreviated 필테 in texts; the standard spelling is 필라테스 (not 필테스 or 파일라테스). The big learner trap is contrasting it with 요가: people will ask 매트(예요), 기구(예요)? — 매트 필라테스 is floor work, 기구 필라테스 uses the reformer machine, and 필라테스 generally targets core strength and posture (자세) whereas 요가 emphasizes flexibility and breathing, so don't call one the other. Note the package culture: lessons come as a 회권 ('N-session ticket'), which you 끊다 — literally 'cut/tear', the same verb as buying a train ticket — never 사다. Sign-up is 등록하다.

mistakes: 10회권을 샀어요. → 10회권을 끊었어요.
For ticketed passes (회권, 정기권) Koreans use 끊다 ('cut/tear off a ticket'), a fixed collocation; 사다 ('buy') sounds unnatural for a session pass.
Say 회권(을) 끊다.
필테스를 해요. → 필라테스를 해요.
The correct transliteration keeps 라: 필라테스. Dropping it (필테스) or adding a vowel (파일라테스) are common spelling slips.
Spell it 필라테스, abbreviate 필테.

usage: verb 하다; 클라이밍(을) 가다 ('go climbing') is just as common
실내(室內) = indoors; almost all city climbing is at indoor gyms
the short-wall, no-rope style most 20-30s actually do
-장(場) marks a sports venue/ground; cf. 운동장, 수영장
examples: 저는 클라이밍을 해요.
I do climbing.
the plain frame; 클라이밍 takes 하다 as its activity verb
주말마다 친구랑 클라이밍 하러 가요.
I go climbing with a friend every weekend.
N마다 = every N; V-(으)러 가다 = go for the purpose of doing
클라이밍장에 암벽화 빌려주는 데 있어요?
Is there somewhere that rents out climbing shoes at the gym?
암벽화(巖壁靴) = climbing shoes; 빌려주다 = to lend out (vs 빌리다 = to borrow)
nuance: 클라이밍 is the English loanword 'climbing'; keep all four syllables — 클라밍 (dropping 이) is a frequent misspelling. The crucial distinction for an English speaker is 클라이밍 vs 등산(登山): 등산 is hiking/ascending an actual mountain on trails, while 클라이밍 is sport climbing up walls or rock faces — Koreans never mix them, so 'I went climbing this weekend' on a hiking trail should be 등산했어요. The trendy gym style is 볼더링 (bouldering: low walls, no rope, just 매트 below), done at an indoor 클라이밍장. Counter vocabulary that helps: 암벽화 (climbing shoes, which you can 빌리다) and 초크 (grip chalk). Beginners always confess 손에 힘이 없다 ('no grip strength').

mistakes: 주말에 클라이밍 갔어요. (meaning a mountain hike) → 주말에 등산 갔어요.
등산 is trail hiking up a mountain; 클라이밍 is technical wall/rock climbing. Using 클라이밍 for a casual mountain walk misdescribes the activity.
Hiking a mountain = 등산; wall/rock climbing = 클라이밍.
클라밍을 해요. → 클라이밍을 해요.
The word transliterates 'climbing' with the 이 kept: 클라이밍. Omitting it is a spelling error.
Keep all syllables: 클라이밍.

usage: use 치다 ('to strike'), the verb for ball/cue/racket games, not 하다
-장(場) = venue; a classic group hangout, often with 당구장 nearby
게임 is the counter for a round; you pay per 게임
-화(靴) = shoes (Sino-Korean); rent these at the counter
examples: 저는 볼링을 잘 못 쳐요.
I'm not very good at bowling.
the simple frame; note 치다 as the verb and 못 + verb = 'can't (do well)'
우리 이따가 볼링 치러 갈래?
Want to go bowling later today?
이따가 = later (within today); -(으)ㄹ래? = casual 'shall we / want to?'
볼링 한 게임에 얼마예요?
How much is one game of bowling?
N에 얼마예요? = how much per N; 에 distributes the price over each unit
nuance: 볼링 is the loanword 'bowling', but the verb is the native 치다 ('to strike/hit'), shared with 당구를 치다, 테니스를 치다 and other implement-and-ball sports — saying 볼링을 하다 marks you as a foreigner. The mental model is: anything you strike with a hand/cue/racket takes 치다, whereas sports you run/play take 하다 (축구를 하다). A 볼링장 (-장 = venue) is a staple group outing and a softer alternative to a drinking 회식. You pay by the 게임 (the counter for a round), and you must swap into rented 볼링화 — the suffix -화(靴) is the Sino-Korean for 'footwear', the same one in 운동화 (sneakers) and 등산화 (hiking boots).

mistakes: 볼링을 해요. → 볼링을 쳐요.
Implement-and-ball games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is the generic 'do' and sounds unnatural for bowling.
Use 볼링을 치다.
운동화 신고 쳐도 돼요? → 볼링화로 갈아 신어야 해요.
Street/athletic shoes (운동화) damage and aren't allowed on the lane; you must change into rented 볼링화.
Rent and wear 볼링화 on the lane.

usage: verb 치다 ('strike'), like other cue/ball games; never 하다
-장(場) = venue; cheap and often open late into the night
the pocketed version; plain 당구 usually means pocketless carom
시간당(時間當) = per hour; the loser often covers the fee
examples: 저는 당구를 못 쳐요.
I can't play billiards.
the basic frame; 못 쳐요 = 'can't play (well)', with the proper verb 치다
친구들이랑 당구 치러 갔어요.
I went to play billiards with friends.
N(이)랑 = casual 'with'; V-(으)러 가다 = go in order to do
당구장은 보통 시간당으로 계산해요.
Billiard halls usually charge by the hour.
시간당 = per hour; 계산하다 = to bill/settle up, also 'to do the math'
nuance: 당구(撞球) is Sino-Korean — 撞 'to strike' + 球 'ball', literally 'strike-ball' — and like other cue sports it takes the verb 치다, not 하다. The classic English-speaker trap is meaning: plain 당구 in Korea usually refers to the pocketless carom games 사구 (four-ball) and 쓰리쿠션 (three-cushion), played by bouncing balls off cushions, NOT the pool you know with six pockets — that pocketed version is specifically 포켓볼. So 'let's play pool' is safest as 당구 치자 only if you mean carom; otherwise specify 포켓볼. A 당구장 (-장 = venue) is a cheap, late-night hangout, traditionally male-coded but now mixed, billed 시간당 (per hour), and the loser customarily pays.

mistakes: 당구를 해요. → 당구를 쳐요.
Cue games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is wrong for 당구 just as it is for 볼링.
Use 당구를 치다.
당구 = pool with pockets (assumed). → 포켓볼 for the pocketed game.
Plain 당구 in Korea defaults to pocketless carom (사구/쓰리쿠션); calling the six-pocket game 당구 without specifying confuses Koreans.
Say 포켓볼 when you mean pocket pool.

usage: games take 하다 (to do/play), never 보다 ('watch')
a pay-by-time cafe stocked with games; locals shorten it to 보드카페
룰 = rules (loanword); staff often explain the game for you
N이서 = '(as a group) of N'; 둘이서, 셋이서, 넷이서 …
examples: 저는 보드게임을 좋아해요.
I like board games.
the simple frame; 보드게임 is a plain object of 좋아하다
이 보드게임 룰이 좀 복잡해요.
The rules of this board game are a bit complicated.
복잡하다(複雜) = complicated, the descriptive verb here; 좀 softens the complaint
넷이서 할 수 있는 보드게임 추천해 주세요.
Please recommend a board game four people can play.
V-(으)ㄹ 수 있는 = that can be done; 추천하다(推薦) = to recommend
nuance: 보드게임 is 'board game' (보드 + 게임). Like all games it takes the verb 하다 ('do/play'), and the trap for English speakers is the verb 'play': there is no all-purpose 'play' in Korean — you 하다 a board game but you 치다 ball games and 켜다/연주하다 instruments, so reaching for one English verb fails. The cultural anchor is the 보드게임 카페 (commonly shortened 보드카페), where you pay by time and staff teach the 룰. It's a cheap date or rainy-day group activity for 20-30s. Don't confuse the game with its parts: the physical board is a 게임판, while 보드게임 names the whole game, and 보드 alone can also mean a snowboard/skateboard, so keep the full 보드게임.

mistakes: 보드게임을 봐요. → 보드게임을 해요.
English 'play a game' tempts learners toward 보다 ('watch') or a literal calque; games are done with 하다.
Use 보드게임을 하다.
우리 보드 하자. → 우리 보드게임 하자.
Bare 보드 is ambiguous (it can mean a snowboard/skateboard); say the full 보드게임 for the tabletop game.
Keep the full word 보드게임.

usage: the activity verb is 하다; you 'do' a room, not 'watch' it
the full venue name; often shortened to 방탈
테마 = each themed room you book; 공포 테마 = a horror room
쓰다 = to use; staff give 힌트 when you're stuck
examples: 저는 방탈출을 좋아해요.
I like escape rooms.
the basic frame; 방탈출 as a plain object of 좋아하다
우리 이번 주말에 방탈출 하러 갈까?
Shall we go do an escape room this weekend?
V-(으)러 가다 = go to do; -(으)ㄹ까? = soft 'shall we?' to a friend
이 테마 너무 어려워서 결국 탈출 못 했어요.
This room was so hard we couldn't escape in the end.
결국(結局) = in the end; 탈출(脫出)하다 = to escape; -아서 gives the reason
nuance: 방탈출 is a transparent compound: 방 'room' + 탈출(脫出) 'escape/break-out' (脫 'shed/escape' + 出 'go out'), i.e. 'room escape'. Write it solid as 방탈출 (the set activity noun), not 방 탈출 with a space, and it's commonly clipped to 방탈. The verb is 하다 — the pitfall is English 'do an escape room' vs the false friend 보다: you never 방탈출을 보다 ('watch'), you 하다 (participate in) it. Inside, each scenario is a 테마 you book ahead; you can request a 힌트 when stuck, and the scary ones are 공포 테마. Don't confuse the noun 탈출 (the act of escaping, used in 탈출하다) with the venue word 방탈출 (the game itself). A staple group outing for young adults.

mistakes: 방탈출을 봤어요. → 방탈출을 했어요.
It's a participatory game: you 하다 (do) it. 보다 ('watch') treats it like a show, which is wrong.
Use 방탈출을 하다.
방 탈출 하러 가자. → 방탈출 하러 가자.
As the name of the activity it is one set word, 방탈출 (or clipped 방탈); inserting a space reads as the literal phrase 'escape the room'.
Write it solid: 방탈출.

usage: 예매(豫買) = advance ticket purchase, distinct from 예약 (reservation)
배우(俳優) = actor; fans choose shows by which performer is cast
examples: 저는 뮤지컬을 좋아해요.
I like musicals.
the simplest frame; 뮤지컬 as object of 좋아하다
대학로에서 뮤지컬 한 편 봤어요.
I saw a musical in Daehangno.
대학로 = Seoul's theater district; 편(編) is the counter for a work/show
주말 공연은 표가 금방 매진돼요.
Weekend shows sell out fast.
매진(賣盡)되다 = to sell out (lit. 'selling exhausted'); 금방 = soon/quickly
nuance: 뮤지컬 is the loanword 'musical', watched with the verb 보다 ('see'), like 영화를 보다 or 공연을 보다 — never 하다 unless you mean performing in it. The sharp contrast to learn is 뮤지컬 vs 연극(演劇): 연극 is a straight (spoken) play, while a 뮤지컬 is sung-through with songs and dance, so don't translate English 'play/theater' as 뮤지컬 by default. Korea has a huge scene centered on 대학로 (Daehangno) and big theaters, and fans pick shows by the 뮤지컬 배우 in the cast. The ticketing pitfall: use 예매하다 — 豫 'in advance' + 買 'buy' — for buying show tickets, NOT 예약하다 (豫約 'reserve'), which is for tables and rooms. Hot dates 매진되다 (sell out) quickly.

The sharp contrast to learn is 뮤지컬 vs 연극(演劇): 연극 is a straight (spoken) play, while a 뮤지컬 is sung-through with songs and dance, so don't translate English 'play/theater' as 뮤지컬 by default.
The ticketing pitfall: use 예매하다 — 豫 'in advance' + 買 'buy' — for buying show tickets, NOT 예약하다 (豫約 'reserve'), which is for tables and rooms.

mistakes: 뮤지컬을 예약했어요. → 뮤지컬을 예매했어요.
Tickets you buy in advance use 예매(豫買, 'pre-buy'); 예약(豫約, 'reserve') is for restaurants/hotels, not performance tickets.
Use 예매하다 for show tickets.
연극이랑 뮤지컬은 같은 거예요. → 뮤지컬은 노래로 하는 공연이에요.
연극 is a spoken play; a 뮤지컬 is sung-through with music and dance. Treating them as identical mislabels the genre.
Distinguish 연극 (play) from 뮤지컬 (musical).

usage: the standard outing phrase; 에 marks the destination
verb 보다, like other things you view/watch
-전(展) is the suffix for a themed show, shorter than -전시회
관람료(觀覽料) = viewing fee; many shows are 무료 (free)
examples: 저는 전시회를 자주 봐요.
I see exhibitions often.
the basic frame; 전시회 as object of 보다, with 자주 = 'often'
주말에 친구랑 사진 전시회 보러 갔어요.
I went to see a photo exhibition with a friend on the weekend.
V-(으)러 가다 = go in order to see; a popular low-key date
이 전시회는 무료라서 사람이 엄청 많아요.
This exhibition is free, so there are a ton of people.
무료(無料) = free of charge; -라서 = 'because (it is)'; 엄청 = a ton (casual)
nuance: 전시회 is Sino-Korean — 展示 'display/exhibit' (展 'spread out' + 示 'show') + 會 'gathering/event' — i.e. a (usually temporary) exhibition event you 보러 가다, a go-to casual outing or date for 20-30s, especially as a 사진전 (photo show) or 미술전 (art show), where -전(展) is the compact suffix. The key learner pitfall is 전시회 vs 미술관(美術館): a 전시회 is the *event* (it opens and closes on dates), whereas a 미술관 is the *building/museum* that houses it — don't say 전시회 when you mean the institution. On fees, art shows usually charge a 관람료 ('viewing fee'), not the generic 입장료 ('entry fee') used at amusement parks; look for 무료 shows, and many offer a 도슨트 (docent-guided tour).

mistakes: 미술관에서 새 전시회가 생겼어요 (meaning the museum). → 전시회 is the event, 미술관 is the building.
전시회 names a temporary show with start/end dates; the permanent venue is a 미술관/갤러리. Swapping them confuses event with place.
Event = 전시회; building = 미술관/갤러리.
전시회 입장료가 얼마예요? → 전시회 관람료가 얼마예요?
For art/photo shows the fee is idiomatically 관람료 ('viewing fee'); 입장료 ('entry fee') fits theme parks and venues, not exhibitions.
Use 관람료 for exhibitions.

usage: to go to a karaoke room
the standard outing phrase; the venue takes 가다
a pay-per-song booth, shortened to 코노; cheap and solo-friendly
곡(曲) = the counter for songs; 부르다 = to sing, not 하다
the free minutes staff add at the end if you ask
examples: 저는 노래방을 좋아해요.
I like karaoke rooms.
the simple frame; the place 노래방 as object of 좋아하다
2차로 노래방 가자!
Let's go to karaoke for round two!
2차(次) = the next stop on a night out; 로 marks 노래방 as the chosen next venue
요즘은 혼자 코노 가서 스트레스 풀어요.
These days I go to coin karaoke alone to de-stress.
스트레스(를) 풀다 = to relieve stress; 코노 = 코인 노래방
nuance: 노래방 is a pure Korean compound: 노래 'song' + 방 'room' = 'song room', a private karaoke booth that is core Korean nightlife and the classic 2차 ('second round') after dinner or drinks. The big pitfall is calling it 가라오케 (karaoke): in Korea 가라오케 sounds dated or implies a pricey hostess bar with staff, so the everyday booth you rent with friends is always 노래방, and the cheap solo version is 코인 노래방 (코노). Verb-wise, you don't 하다 a song — you 부르다 ('sing') a 곡, where 곡(曲) is the proper counter (한 곡, 두 곡). A nice extra to know: you can plead 서비스 시간 넣어 주세요 to get free bonus minutes from staff.

Use 노래방 (or 코노) for the ordinary karaoke room.
노래 한 곡 했어요. → 노래 한 곡 불렀어요.
Songs are sung with 부르다, not done with 하다; 곡 is the counter you pair with 부르다.
Use 노래를 부르다 / 한 곡 부르다.

usage: the standard outing phrase; the venue takes 가다
the matching shirt-and-shorts set they hand you to wear
수면(睡眠) = sleep + 실(室) = room; you can stay overnight in many
the signature snack-bar drink, paired with 삶은 계란 (boiled eggs)
examples: 저는 찜질방을 좋아해요.
I like jjimjilbang.
the basic frame; the place as object of 좋아하다
주말에 찜질방 가서 푹 쉬었어요.
I went to a jjimjilbang on the weekend and rested deeply.
푹 쉬다 = to rest fully/deeply, the whole point of going; -아서 chains the two actions
밤새 찜질방에서 자도 돼요?
Is it okay to sleep at the jjimjilbang all night?
밤새 = all night long; V-아/어도 돼요? = 'is it okay to …?'
nuance: 찜질방 is a Korean compound: 찜질 'applying heat/a hot compress' + 방 'room' — a 24-hour heated sauna/spa complex where you change into a 찜질복, sweat in heated 한증막 rooms, snack on 식혜 with 삶은 계란, and can even sleep over in a 수면실. The pitfall is treating it as a synonym of 목욕탕(沐浴湯): a 목욕탕 is a plain public bathhouse for washing/soaking in hot tubs, whereas a 찜질방 adds the dry heated 찜질 rooms, communal lounge areas, food, and overnight sleeping — much bigger in scope. Also note 찜질방 (the venue) vs 사우나 (a sauna, which may be just a sweat room inside a 목욕탕 or hotel). A cheap, very Korean way to relax or crash for the night.

Say 찜질방 when you want the sauna-spa complex.
제 옷 입고 들어가도 돼요? → 찜질복으로 갈아입어야 해요.
In the common areas you wear the provided matching 찜질복, not your own clothes.
Change into the 찜질복.

usage: 가입하다(加入) = to sign up/join an organization; takes 에
any hobby + 동호회 names an adult interest group
정기(定期) = scheduled/regular; clubs gather on a set day
회비(會費) = the fee members chip in to run the group
examples: 저는 등산 동호회에 가입했어요.
I joined a hiking club.
the basic frame; 동호회 + 에 + 가입하다, the fixed 'join' pattern
동호회 회비가 한 달에 만 원이에요.
The club dues are 10,000 won a month.
한 달에 = per month; 회비 framed as a recurring monthly cost
이 동호회는 직장인들이 많아요.
This club has a lot of working professionals.
직장인(職場人) = office worker/professional, a common club demographic
nuance: 동호회(同好會) is Sino-Korean — 同 'same' + 好 'liking' + 會 'association', literally 'a society of people who like the same thing': an adult hobby/interest club (sports, photography, hiking) that is the main way working 20-30s meet people outside the office. The sharp contrast to learn is 동호회 vs 동아리: a 동아리 is a school/university circle for students, while adults join a 동호회, so don't use 동아리 for your office tennis group. Also distinguish the lasting, organized 동호회 from a one-off 모임 (a single get-together/meeting). Verb-wise you 가입하다 ('join/sign up', 加入) — not the literal 들어가다 ('go inside') — then pay 회비 (dues) and attend the 정기 모임.

mistakes: 회사 동아리에 가입했어요 (an adult club). → 회사 동호회에 가입했어요.
동아리 is specifically a school/college circle; adult interest clubs are 동호회. Using 동아리 for a grown-ups' group sounds off.
Adults' club = 동호회; students' circle = 동아리.
동호회를 들어갔어요. → 동호회에 가입했어요.
Joining an organization uses 가입하다 with the particle 에; the literal 들어가다 ('enter a space') doesn't fit membership.
Use 동호회에 가입하다.
